description: I'm Tharun Kumar V, AI/ML developer (B.E. CSE, AI & ML) and open researcher at Cohere Labs. Built DamageScope, a post-disaster damage detection system using the BRIGHT dataset, published at IEEE RMKMATE 2026. SARcasm extends it to SAR data, speckle noise, backscatter, and change detection. Need data analysis/stats, a web developer for the dashboard, and an Earth science background is a bonus.
summary: FloodLive is an interactive, open-source web app that visualizes surface change using two real NISAR L-band acquisitions over [AREA]. A before/after slider, HH/HV toggle, change map and statistics show where radar backscatter rose or fell, with every number traced to its source granule. It makes NISAR data accessible to non-experts and shows how radar sees through monsoon cloud when optical satellites cannot, while clearly stating its limits: coarse pixels, no ground truth, and no claim of damage.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

FloodLive is an interactive web app that shows how Earth's surface changed between two real NISAR radar acquisitions over the Chennai region, Tamil Nadu, India. A before/after swipe slider compares the two dates, a change layer shows where radar backscatter rose or fell (in dB), and a statistics panel reports the area changed in km2, the mean change, and the distribution of changes. A provenance panel lists the exact NISAR granule IDs, dates, track, frame, pass direction and polarizations, all read from the data files, so every number can be checked.

HOW IT WORKS

We selected two NISAR L-band GCOV (Level-2 geocoded polarimetric covariance) acquisitions with the same track, frame and pass direction, which is required for valid change detection: 04.11.2026 and 10.11.2026. A Python pipeline reads the HH and HV backscatter, clips to the study area, converts to dB, applies speckle filtering, and computes post-minus-pre change. Changes beyond +/-[3] dB are classified as increase or decrease. The results are exported as georeferenced overlays and JSON and served by a static website. Between the two dates, heavy northeast-monsoon rain from cyclone Murasu hit Chennai around 1-2 November 2026. We interpret changes as hypotheses (soil moisture, standing water, vegetation change) and say so on the page.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Radar sees through cloud, which is when optical satellites fail during monsoon and cyclone events. The tool turns hard-to-read HDF5 radar data into a visual comparison that planners, students and the public can explore without GIS skills. We hope it helps people understand what NISAR reveals and shows a reusable, open-source workflow for turning NISAR products into accessible change maps.

TOOLS

Data: NISAR L2 GCOV via NASA ASF DAAC / Earthdata. Python (h5py, NumPy, rasterio, asf_search/earthaccess) for processing. React, Vite, Leaflet and Recharts for the interface, deployed on Vercel, code on GitHub. [ADD: Sentinel-2 / Meteomatics / Planetary Computer ONLY if actually used.] AI coding assistants ([NAMES]) were used to help write code and text; we reviewed and tested the outputs.

WHAT'S CREATIVE

We focused on honest communication: provenance for every number, plain-language explanations of why water looks dark and flooded vegetation can look bright in radar, and a clear methods and limitations page. The app refuses to build for production if placeholder data is present, so nothing shown is simulated.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Same-track pairing so changes reflect the ground, not look-angle differences; coarse pixel size (tens of meters), so we map areas, not buildings; wet-soil, vegetation and urban double-bounce effects; no ground truth, so we describe change in backscatter and do not claim flood extent or damage. [ADD: validation against X, if done.] Future work: longer time series as the NISAR archive grows, soil-moisture and subsidence layers, automated pipelines, and more events.
